title: Shortest common superstring in \(O^*(1.99^n)\) time
formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic classical word-RAM algorithm \(A\), a constant \(K>0\), and integers \(d\ge2\) and \(a\ge1\) such that, for every list of \(n\ge0\) explicitly given finite strings over any finite alphabet, \(A\) outputs a shortest common superstring within \(K(199/100)^n(L+1)^a\) machine steps? Here \(L\) is the total binary input length, and words have \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil)\) bits. The constant base \(199/100\) is fixed, independently of all string lengths and alphabet sizes.
why: The problem asks whether the classical exponential cost of ordering many overlapping strings can be reduced by a fixed factor in the exponent. It is a central exact-algorithm question for sequence assembly and helps distinguish the complexity of string overlap from more general ordering problems.
status_note: Source-open in Kulikov’s 2013 seminar question and the 2019 unrestricted exact-algorithms discussion. A bounded check through 2026-09-16 found no verified resolution of the retained deterministic classical 1.99^n branch. Bounded-string-length, quantum and approximation results have different assumptions or guarantees.

progress.text: The seminar report asks for an \(O^*(1.99^n)\) exact algorithm on unrestricted strings, alongside distinct bounded-length and reduction questions.
A randomized faster-than-base-two exact algorithm is obtained for every fixed maximum input-string length.
The unrestricted fixed-improvement question is stated again in the paper’s exact-algorithms discussion.
A bounded-error quantum result is reported for the paper’s equal-length formulation and quantum-query cost convention; it does not establish the classical target.
New reported general and greedy approximation guarantees concern a different objective from exact running time.

sentences: Shortest common superstring asks for a shortest string containing every input string as a contiguous substring.
The parameter n counts input strings, while their full encoded lengths contribute only a fixed polynomial factor to the target running time.
The selected question asks for a uniform deterministic classical algorithm with the literal exponential base 1.99 posed in the seminar report.
String lengths and alphabet sizes are unrestricted, and the output must attain the exact optimum.
Faster algorithms for bounded-length strings, quantum speedups and approximation advances do not settle this classical exact target.

definitions:
The alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}\), where \(\sigma\ge1\) is supplied with the input and \(\sigma\le\max\{1,\sum_i|s_i|\}\). This is a representation convention: arbitrary finite input alphabets can be relabeled by consecutive integers without changing the number of strings, containment, or optimum output length. A string is an explicitly listed finite sequence of alphabet symbols. A string \(s\) is a substring of \(z\) if \(z=u s v\) for finite strings \(u,v\); its occurrence must be contiguous. A common superstring of \(s_1,\ldots,s_n\) contains every \(s_i\) as a substring. It is shortest if no common superstring has fewer symbols. The output must be an actual shortest superstring, not just a superstring of approximately optimal length. Multiple optimum outputs are allowed. For \(n=0\), the optimum is the empty string.

For definiteness, encode a nonnegative integer \(z\) by \(1^b0\,\operatorname{bin}(z)\), where \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\), other binary numerals have no leading zeroes, and \(b\) is the numeral length. The input consists of these codes for \(\sigma,n\), followed, for each string in order, by a code for its length and then its symbols in \(h=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2\sigma\rceil\}\) bits each. Every encoded symbol must be less than \(\sigma\). The concatenation has \(L\) bits, with no trailing data. The output uses the same length-and-symbol convention. The parameter \(n\) is the number of strings in this supplied list, before any algorithmic preprocessing; it is not the total number of symbols or the maximum string length. Empty strings, duplicates and strings contained in others are permitted. There is no bound on the maximum string length in terms of \(n\), no fixed-alphabet restriction, and no promise on pairwise overlaps.

The RAM receives \(n,L\) in designated input registers in addition to the encoded input. It has a fixed finite program, a constant number of registers and random-access words indexed by \(w\)-bit addresses. Its word operations are copying, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), bitwise Boolean operations, shifts with discarded overflow, unsigned comparison and conditional branching. A shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Reading or writing one addressed memory word, reading an input word or writing an output word costs one step, as does each arithmetic or control instruction. Input bits are packed into words and padded with zeroes beyond the known input length \(L\); padding is not part of the input. Words initially outside the input and fixed initialization are zero. Values exceeding one word must be represented by multiple words with all operations charged. There is no unbounded unit-cost arithmetic, nonuniform advice, oracle, randomness or quantum operation. The program and constants \(K,d,a\) do not depend on \(n,L,\sigma\) or the input strings. All parsing, preprocessing, memory accesses and output writing count. No separate polynomial-space requirement is imposed. The bound is worst-case for every valid input.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of such an algorithm and fixed constants, including exact optimality of every output and the stated uniform worst-case resource bound, or a complete Lean proof of their logical negation in the selected machine model. A result only for a fixed maximum input-string length, a quantum algorithm, a polynomial-time approximation, or a larger fixed exponential base does not establish this target. A conditional lower bound alone does not establish unconditional nonexistence.

context_blocks.text: The main question in the 2013 seminar report is the literal bound \(O^*(1.99^n)\), where \(n\) counts input strings. This card selects that first question and makes a deterministic classical word-RAM interpretation explicit because the short source does not specify randomization or a detailed machine. The report also asks separate questions about bounded-length strings and a reduction from Traveling Salesman.

The known baseline is \(O^*(2^n)\), with the star suppressing a fixed polynomial in total input length. The 2013 report states that polynomial space is possible at this baseline; it does not require polynomial space of the requested faster algorithm.

Golovnev, Kulikov and Mihajlin give a randomized algorithm for strings of length at most a fixed \(r\), with time \(O^*(2^{(1-1/(2r^2+1))n})\). Its improvement depends on the length bound, which is absent from the main question.

The 2019 paper again asks for an exact classical \(O^*((2-\varepsilon)^n)\) algorithm for unrestricted strings and fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). This broader question supplies later dated context; it does not replace the particular \(1.99\) threshold retained here.

Khadiev and Bosch Machado report a bounded-error quantum \(O^*(1.728^n)\) bound. Their Section 2.1 formulates equal-length input strings, and Section 2.2 defines quantum query cost as running time. This does not establish the unrestricted classical bound with all machine work charged.

An August 2026 preprint reports a \(7/3\)-approximation for general shortest common superstring and a factor \(3\) guarantee for the greedy algorithm. These concern approximation quality, not the exact exponential-time target.

checked_sources: Read the original cached Dagstuhl report, Section 6.2, printed page 60 (page 21 of the standalone PDF), and Section 5.13, printed page 54. The first question has literal base 1.99 and n is the number of input strings. Bounded-length strings and an n-preserving TSP reduction are distinct follow-up questions. No randomization convention, machine model, fixed alphabet or space restriction is specified for the desired algorithm.

Read Golovnev, Kulikov and Mihajlin’s author PDF: introduction, Theorem 1, Theorem 3 and Section 5, Further Directions. Theorem 3 is randomized, with exponent (1−1/(2r²+1))n for fixed maximum string length r; Theorem 1 explicitly permits false negatives. Theorem 3 and Section 5 are on author-PDF page 6. Polynomial factors refer to total input length. The introduction states a binary-alphabet transfer attributed to Vassilevska (2005); that reduction proof was not independently checked and is unnecessary for the proposed general-alphabet card.

Read Golovnev, Kulikov, Logunov, Mihajlin and Nikolaev, APPROX/RANDOM 2019, Section 6.1, page 26:16, which explicitly retains the unrestricted fixed-improvement question. The proposed card uses its dated open status but does not copy its suggested approach.

Read Khadiev and Bosch Machado, arXiv:2112.13319v1, 26 December 2021: abstract, introduction, Sections 2.1–2.2, and Theorem 1 with bounded-error analysis on pages 8–9. Section 2.1 stipulates equal input-string lengths, and Section 2.2 explicitly calls quantum query complexity the running time. The report is contextual only: neither unrestricted input lengths nor full classical or quantum machine-work accounting is verified. No independent full quantum-proof audit is claimed.

Read ECCC TR26-157, primary abstract and Section 1, page 1. Reported 7/3 approximation and greedy factor 3 concern approximation rather than exact running time. The page lists submission 27 August 2026 and publication 30 August 2026. Also read the primary abstract of Shibata, arXiv:2609.01365v1, 1 September 2026: its claimed greedy lower bound of 9/4 likewise does not address exact running time; no proof audit or edit to the related greedy card was performed.

Bounded subsequent searches through 16 September 2026 for general exact classical shortest-superstring algorithms and the 1.99^n target found no matching resolution. This supports a dated source-open status with explicit review limits, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

The deterministic classical word-RAM branch is an explicit editorial interpretation approved by the parent reviewer. Word size d(n+ceil(log2(L+2))) permits exponential addressing while charging all RAM operations. No equivalence to strict multitape Turing-machine running time is asserted. Alphabet relabeling and explicit binary encoding preserve string count and exact optimum length; no fixed alphabet is imposed.

Preserved importance 69 and the existing category. The numeric threshold 199/100 is a resource-bound base, while the requested output is an exact optimization witness; this is a yes/no algorithm-existence question, not a numerical benchmark target subject to additive output tolerance.
